children: State Bank of India is exploring lending models based on future cash flows as new-age businesses often lack the traditional collateral required for bank finance

Cash-flow-based lending is set to become increasingly important for financing new-age industries such as data centres, solar manufacturing and technology-driven businesses, State Bank of India Managing Director Ashwini Kumar Tewari said on Friday.

Speaking at a financial market conclave hosted by the Bombay Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Tewari said banks need to develop new lending models as emerging businesses may not have the tangible security traditionally required for bank finance.

“Unless banks are able to find ways to fund these kinds of new businesses,” banks will need to move beyond relying only on collateral, Tewari said, pointing to sectors such as pharmaceuticals and technology.

Tewari said State Bank of India (SBI) is already evaluating cash-flow-based lending and applying the approach to emerging sectors. The bank calls its model CHAKRA, which it is using to assess businesses where conventional security may not be adequate.
The approach requires lenders to assess a business based on its expected revenue and ability to generate cash rather than relying primarily on physical assets as collateral.

Tewari said this could become particularly relevant for businesses such as data centres, solar manufacturing and other technology-led industries, where the underlying assets and business models can differ significantly from traditional industries.
Technology Assessment Key To Lending Decisions

However, financing such businesses also presents challenges for banks. Tewari said lenders need to understand the technology involved, its revenue potential and the economics of the project before deciding on financing.

He cited the solar sector as an example, saying SBI had examined the technology used in projects and found that some technologies were already outdated. Different technologies can also have different power-generation economics, making it difficult for banks to assess the likely revenue and cash-flow generation of a project.
The ability to establish future revenue and cash flows therefore remains a key challenge for lenders looking to expand financing to new-age sectors, Tewari said.
The shift towards cash-flow-based lending could allow banks to finance businesses that have limited traditional collateral but have identifiable revenue streams and viable operating models.
